questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy has sudden scrotal pain. At surgery the testis is twisted, dark red, and swollen. Why is the infarct hemorrhagic?

options.A: Arterial occlusion in an end-arterial organ
options.B: Septic embolus to the testicular artery
options.D: Venous obstruction with ongoing arterial inflow

questions.explanation: Torsion first compresses thin-walled veins; arterial inflow continues → blood pools → red infarct. A: End-arterial arterial occlusion gives white infarcts. B: No sign of infection; an arterial embolus would give a white infarct. C: Liquefactive necrosis is typical of brain/abscess, not a cause of hemorrhage. E: Arterial thrombosis in a solid organ gives a white infarct.

questions.stem: Which organ most typically develops a pale (white), wedge-shaped infarct after arterial embolism?
questions.explanation: Solid organs with end-arterial supply (kidney, spleen, heart) form white infarcts. B: Lung has dual supply → red infarcts. C: Small intestine has dual supply → red. D: Ovary infarcts are venous (torsion) → red. E: Brain infarcts become liquefactive.

questions.stem: A patient with severe thrombocytopenia has many 1–2 mm red spots on the skin of the legs. What are these lesions?
questions.explanation: Pinpoint 1–2 mm hemorrhages are petechiae. A: Purpura are 3–10 mm. B: Ecchymoses are > 1 cm bruises. C: Hematomas are localized collections within tissue. D: Telangiectasias are dilated vessels, not hemorrhages.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old has black, tarry stools for 3 days. What is the most likely bleeding site?
questions.explanation: Melena = partially digested blood, usually from an upper GI source such as a duodenal ulcer. A: Sigmoid → hematochezia. C: Rectum → hematochezia. D: Anal canal → bright red blood. E: Left colon bleeding → hematochezia.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old with atrial fibrillation dies suddenly 6 hours after a large embolic occlusion of a coronary artery. At autopsy, microscopy of the territory shows no definite necrosis. What best explains this?

options.A: The occlusion was not hemodynamically significant
options.B: Dual blood supply protected the myocardium
options.E: Liquefactive necrosis had dissolved the cells

questions.explanation: Histologic evidence of necrosis lags; death within ~12–18 h may show only congestion or pallor. A: A large occlusion is significant. B: The heart has end-arterial coronary supply. D: Myocytes don't regenerate. E: Myocardium undergoes coagulative necrosis.

questions.stem: Two patients have complete occlusion of the same coronary branch. In patient 1 it developed slowly over years; in patient 2 it occurred suddenly from an embolus. Only patient 2 has a large infarct. What best explains the difference?

options.A: Patient 1 has a dual coronary blood supply
options.B: Collaterals had time to enlarge in patient 1
options.D: Venous outflow was obstructed in patient 2

questions.explanation: Slow narrowing allows time for collateral vessels to enlarge; sudden occlusion leaves little time to compensate. A: The heart is an end-arterial organ in both. C: Both have the same tissue type. D: Embolism is arterial, not venous. E: Myocytes don't regenerate enough to prevent infarction.

questions.stem: A bruise on the thigh changes from red-blue to green over several days. Which pigment produces the green color?
questions.explanation: Ecchymosis colors follow hemoglobin breakdown: red-blue/purple, then green (biliverdin), then yellow-brown (bilirubin and hemosiderin). A: Bilirubin gives yellow-brown later. B: Hemosiderin contributes to the late yellow-brown. C: Hemoglobin gives the initial red-blue. E: Lipofuscin is a wear-and-tear pigment, unrelated.
